assumptions: you accept an existing clinical formula rather than fitting your own, so coefficients are copied from a paper
you have users willing to connect real blood panels, since without panels the score is wearable noise
no regulatory clearance is implied; a consumer dashboard, not a diagnostic device
clone_cost.estimate: about a week for the pipeline, longer for anything you would defend clinically
clone_cost.why: Reading the published PhenoAge formula and applying nine lab values is a day's work; HealthKit and Health Connect auth plus a Gemini schema-constrained PDF pass is another few. The part that does not come free is a labelled corpus to know your parser is right, and any claim about reversing aging.

hazard_note: A biological-age score computed from a mortality model, presented to consumers with weekly supplement and protocol recommendations, and a roadmap that plans to predict how interventions shift the curve. Nothing on the page frames the output as non-medical, and no clinician review, cohort or validation is mentioned for the score its interface is built around.

prior_art.relation: same architecture of trust - a published clinical score presented through a calm UI with an escalation-style recommendation loop - and the same unmeasured gap between a computed index and validated guidance.

opposite end of the same problem: Medvoice closes a loop on an action the patient confirms, while this one opens a recommendation loop with no adherence signal at all. Comparing them shows what a verification step buys.

what_breaks_first: Trust in the score, the moment it moves for a reason the user can see is unrelated to their behaviour. A PhenoAge output is dominated by blood chemistry that changes quarterly, while the weekly loop promises movement from sleep and steps, so the dashboard's cadence and the model's sensitivity disagree; the reported parsing accuracy cannot rescue it either, since a single misread unit becomes a wrong age.
what_to_steal: Force the extraction model into a strict response schema per provider instead of writing per-provider parsers, and keep the raw values alongside the parsed ones; smooth noisy physiological inputs over a short and a long window so a derived score cannot jitter day to day; ship the derived score against a baseline the user already trusts (chronological age) rather than as a bare number.
worth_note: Two pieces are worth taking and one is worth doubting. Grammar-constrained decoding for provider-specific PDF layouts is a real technique for any document pipeline, and smoothing volatile wearable inputs with nested EMAs before feeding a scoring model is the unglamorous fix that makes a score stable enough to display. The product itself sits in a crowded longevity-dashboard category whose hardest part - whether the number means anything - is exactly where the page offers a percentage with no denominator.
